utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. And before I proceed, we are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis today. Judge Stole being constrained to leave early because of a family matter, and that will be the positioning as well tomorrow. All the accused are here. Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer. From the Defence teams, I only notice the absence of Mr. Ostojic and Mr. Lazarevic. So we can start. Good morning, everybody. But I understand, Madam Fauveau, that you have a preliminary. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is to inform the Trial Chamber and the parties that we had a scheduling issue, not with the upcoming witness Mr. Velo Pajic, but as far as the next witness is concerned who for family reasons needs to be at home on Monday. So it will be Ratko Milijanovic as the next witness, and then we may ask witness Stojanovic to come back again. If need be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Ms. Fauveau, and I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also have another motion I would like to submit to you. Yesterday, when we prepared the witness Velo Pajic, he drew a sketch of the underground building which the previous witness had mentioned also. Just to avoid wasting any time during the hearing, I would like you to authorise me to add this sketch which he drew yesterday in front of us to our 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Is there any objection from you, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: None, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And from the other Defence teams? None. So permission is granted. Let's bring in the witness. In the meantime, please be informed we will finish at 1.15 so that we -- We will finish at 1.15 today, so that we can attend the swearing-in ceremony of Judge Christoph Flugge. Same will happen tomorrow. I understand Mr. Josse will be -- Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Understandably, the legal officer has been very helpful in liaising with me about this. I haven't, in fact, been around all my learned friends, that's my fault, and there are two I haven't spoken to. So far, everyone else I have spoken to is agreeable to rising a bit early tomorrow so that my client and perhaps others can celebrate a feast day in prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. This is what I was precisely going to say. Mr. Josse will be liaising with everyone and will -- can communicate to you that we will be rising at 1.15 as well tomorrow, between 1.15 and 1.30 anyway. How the sitting itself will be spread out, we are still discussing amongst ourselves, and we'll let you know in due course how it's going to be today and how it's going to be tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I will revert to Ms. Fino later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Good morning, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Has anyone tried to contact you on the subject matter of your testimony between yesterday and today, tried to speak to you or something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nobody did, Your Honour. I was really very lonely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I think you will be lonely today as well, because I don't anticipate seeing you to finish your testimony completely today. So let's continue, Ms. Fauveau. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, yesterday, we started talking about the Spreca operation. In the period before the operation, did officers of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska come to the area of your corps?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Ms. Fauveau, in case you aren't finished by the time, break will be at 10.20 and not at 10.30, and it will be a shortened break. Instead of 25 minutes, we will have a 20 minute break. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was just before the Spreca operation started?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Milovanovic was there because we had operations on Majevica, and he came to see how this was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show you 5D1277. These are conversations that were tapped by Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did General Milovanovic arrive in the area of your corps? Did it coincide with this date, i.e., the 20th of March 1995?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can't say with any degree of certainty that it was exactly that date, but he was there during that period; maybe one or two days earlier, one or two days later, but I can affirm that he was on Majevica.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show you page 3 of this document. This is still the 20th of March 1995 at 2205, and we can see that General Milovanovic informs General Mladic, who is in Belgrade, about the situation in Vlasic and Majevica.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: If General Milovanovic, during this conversation, was in the area of your corps, how easy was it for him to contact General Mladic in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's technically feasible without any difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show you document 5D974; 5D.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said that your corps had planned the Spreca operation. Do you recognise this particular document?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise this document. It originates from my corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order for attack, i.e., an order for the part of the operations that my part of the corps was involved in.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You already mentioned that the administration for operations and training of the Main Staff was not involved in the planning of the operations at an operational level. As far as this particular operation is concerned, i.e., Spreca, and this particular order, did the operation -- did the administration for operations and training of the Main Staff have any influence over or did it play any role in the drafting of this order?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order of the East Bosnian Corps and it was carried out by my command, had nothing to do with the operations organ save for having incorporated the original document which was the directive.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I think that yesterday we saw another document, not only the directive but another document, which was a follow-up document.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you. The directive and the order for combat operations. Those are original documents based on which and on the situation on the ground this order was drafted for Spreca operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: After this order was drafted, did any orders come from the Main Staff regarding the Spreca operation?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that I had to coordinate this with the command of the Drina Corps. I met up with my colleague, General Zivanovic. I believe that General Milovanovic was present when I was coordinating this activity with the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show you Exhibit 5D978; 78.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you remember anything about this order?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. This was more tied to the problem of Drvar airport. Every day, several transport or cargo planes landed there; and according to our information, they brought arms and weapons and equipment for the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In item 2 of this order, we can see that Drvar could be open to only on the orders of or with the approval of the commander or the Chief of Staff of the army of the Republika Srpska. Was this customary in the army of the Republika Srpska that only the commander and the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff can give such an order or such an approval?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, every unit had control over its activity. The Main Staff had rocket units and it had an airforce. And, here, we are ordered not to use our artillery until we are -- they approved that. I believe that they had their own goal, that's why they ordered us that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: A while ago, you mentioned coordination between the Eastern Bosnia Corps and the Drina Corps. You mentioned the fact that General Milovanovic was involved in this coordination, or, at any rate, he was present during the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show you 5D979.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: As you can see in this document, it is the commander of the Drina Corps who is asking you to forward information on to General Milovanovic. Can you explain to us why the commander of the Drina Corps was asking you to forward this information on to General Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, General Milovanovic was deployed at the command post of the Majevica tactical group of the East Bosnian Corps on Mount Majevica, and the telegram could go to him through the Main Staff and then they would have to return it to us; or, also, it could have been sent directly to my command with a request for him to be informed. General Zivanovic opted for the shorter route, and asked me to inform General Milovanovic about this telegram.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: If you look at the he second paragraph, at the end of the second paragraph of this document, it says in this part of the document: "I will designate persons who will wait in Standard barracks and conduct Lieutenant-General Milovanovic my observation post." Can you tell us where these barracks were, the Standard barracks?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Standard was a building of a former factory at the exit from the town of Zvornik, and that's where the command of the Zvornik Brigade was. Generally, Zivanovic, and some of his officers, were at their IKM, i.e., at the observation post. General Milovanovic was not aware of its coordinates, and that's why General Zivanovic informed him that a person would be waiting for him and bring him to the observation post to help him get his bearings.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You mentioned a while ago the coordination between the Eastern Bosnia Corps and the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show you document 5D981.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This is a document which comes from the Drina Corps and which was sent to General Milovanovic and to him personally. This has to do with the Eastern Bosnia Corps, as you can see, which is mentioned often times in this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to draw the attention of the Bench to the fact that there is a mistake on one of the pages of this document in English. It says "General Milovanovic" [as interpreted]. In fact, it is "General Milovanovic" in the B/C/S version. In English, it says "General Milanovic." It should read "General Milovanovic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed. Thank you, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to show you page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's also on page 2 in English and in B/C/S we are talking about the first paragraph. In English, we are talking about the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: "The Main Staff of the VRS, as its capacities allow, appoint an officer who will seek to coordinate and ensure the uniformity and simultaneous of the engagement of the forces for more than three corps in the operation." Is it right that a member of the Main Staff came at a latter stage to coordinate these actions?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there is a mistake here.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did someone from the Main Staff come to coordinate all of this?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There have been two questions here, so let me take them one at a time. Upon the directive and implementation order, this operation had to be commanded by the command of the East Bosnian Corps. In the meantime, the Drina Corps incorporated some of the forces of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps which had not been originally envisaged and which, obviously, did not fully accept the command of the Drina Corps. That is why the command of the Drina Corps asked for somebody to come from the Main Staff as the superior command and to take over the coordination of the operation. Initially, this was done by General Milovanovic; and later on, as far as I can remember, it was Colonel Masal who took over from him.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Since we are talking about coordination, can you tell us how this coordination was done, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Coordination is one of the elements of the command function. In principle, it was carried out by the superior officer, and it is carried out in the following way: Actions are coordinated among several units, according to the territory of engagement, time of engagement, way of engagement, stages of engagement, goals of engagement, and, finally, according to what happens after the end of the operation so as to enable the units to carry out combat operations in a synchronised way in order to achieve a maximum effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can this coordination be done by an officer who remains in his office?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, coordination is carried out from an observation post where at the territory where combat operations are to take place can be seen. There is no point in doing it from an office.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Since we are talking about various actions undertaking during the fighting, can you tell us who was in charge of monitoring the combat operations?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a general question. Combat operations are followed by the one who is commanding. The superior command has the right and often even the duty to send someone from the command to be present at this site, that is, at the command post of this subordinate command; and immediately follow the activities and do what they can for that to take place in a more organised and synchronised fashion; and, if necessary, to engage some elements of the superior command, that is, possibly airforce, et cetera, in order to avoid wasting time by sending telegrams, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you tell us which body, as far as the units of the army of Republika Srpska, were in charge of follow the actions of the enemy forces?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could just have some specificity as to what we're talking about. Units of the VRS, what actions are we talking about? It's a very general question. I am sure the General can answer, but I think it's just helpful to place some specificity on the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you be more specific, Ms. Fauveau, and perhaps break it down, somehow, into various questions - thank you - because I think that's the only way you can do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In an army, I assume it is important to know what the intentions and movements of the enemy forces are.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Knowing the enemy and his forces, his intentions and objectives, is half the success in any war. Following the activities of the enemy is the task of reconnaissance forces or our units, and this information is analysed at one place, and assessment as to their value and accuracy is done by intelligence organs. Only based on such data can activities of our forces be planned, depending on who our enemy is and how they are deployed and what their combat efficiency is. You plan differently if the enemy forces are broken up, and if their morale is poor, then you need not attack; then you can launch another tactical -- tactical activity, and that is chasing the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said that the Chief of Staff, General Milovanovic, was, first of all, in charge of coordination. Where he was he based when he was in charge of coordination?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you may I have noticed that he -- first, he came to me, to the command of the Eastern Bosnia Corps; and, together, we went to the command of the tactical group of Majevica. He acquainted himself with the previous activities that we had launched, and he was able to see that the relay station at the top of Majevica had been liberated. He saw that the units were and where they had been when the cease-fire was agreed. With my commanders, he defined subsequent activities, and then he went to the Drina Corps, where I also went later. The problem was that the unit which had arrived from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps was unwilling to leave the barracks and take the positions from where it was supposed to attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: At some point in the fighting area, was there a forward command post of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially, no. But, upon the request of the commander of the Drina Corps, it was established in the zone of the Drina Corps. I think that Colonel Masal, who later became general, was there permanently, because General Milovanovic, after two or three days, had to leave due to other commitments. He had to go to the Main Staff, as the commander was absent.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show you document 5D986.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: As you can see, this is a combat report of the Eastern Bosnia Corps of the 14th of May, 1995, which had been addressed to the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska and also addressed to the Main Staff of the army of the Republika Srpska, IKM 1, Zvornik. What I am interested in is this: Paragraph 2 of this report, in B/C/S, you can see the abbreviation "NS VRS." Can you tell us what this abbreviation means in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the report, we are saying that the Chief of Staff, that is, the Main Staff - in other words, General Milovanovic - that he was present at our command post.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I believe that you have already said that he was -- that General Milovanovic was able to contact General Mladic in the area of your corps, but can you tell us a little bit more about this. How did General Milovanovic communicate with the other units in the Main Staff when he was in the area of your corps?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, when he is in the zone of some corps, every officer from the Main Staff has at his disposal the entire communications system of that corps, toward the Main Staff and through the Main Staff, with all other units as well. He was able to establish communication by radio, radio relay, teleprinter, military phone lines, protected or secure lines, and even civilian phone lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would now like to move on to another topic and talk about the general situation which prevailed in the area of your corps in 1995. Can you tell us what the situation was like at the beginning of the year?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are talking about the last year of the war, what we didn't know then, but there were indications that it would be the last year. The political leadership had already published that it would agree to a division of the territory of 49 to 51, and this actually prevented us, as commanders, from taking any offensive action. The soldiers at the front, who were already exhausted by combat, were willing to sacrifice to defend the existing territory, but they were not willing to sacrifice in attacks to take new territories. They logically argued that we already have more than we need. If you need additional territories, let's swap with the enemy, let's not die for it. We, as commanders, understood that. We were skeptical about the upcoming operation, Sadjestvo, which was planned, and for exactly this reason: We expected the political leadership to start negotiations to end the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: At that time, I believe you have already mentioned this, but do you remember if there were any agreements that had been signed between the various parties in this war?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there had been several cease-fires. They were mostly initiated by our enemy who was buying time in that way, in using it to -- for supplying themselves with more armaments and ammunition, et cetera. The international community wasn't being sincere with us. We really believed that every cease-fire would eventually turn into peace.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When an agreement on the cease-fire was signed, did the units at a lower level, such as the brigades, receive a copy of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the signing of each agreement was accompanied by an order from the Main Staff about its implementation, and we always received the integral text of the agreement as an annex. That agreement was forwarded to all units, and, at the lowest level, it was read out to the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show you Exhibit 5D1292.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Earlier, you mentioned the orders that accompanied the cease-fire agreement. This is such an order dated 1st of January 1995, and I'd like to refer you to item 4 on page 2. Does this item 4, indeed, reflect the general position that the army of the Republika Srpska took in respect of this cease-fire, this agreement?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In item 4, the commander is making the responsibility of the subordinate commands more stringent. They must respect the rules of the cease-fire, and he forbids the use of some weapons that can be used only if we are attacked. I believe that both the military and the civilian leadership was sincerely in favour of this cease-fire agreement, and the agreement on the cessation of hostilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Turn page 1 of this order.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you just tell us at whom this order was addressed?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order is addressed to the commanders and the chiefs of staff of all units that are subordinate to the Main Staff; that is, the commands of the corps, the airforce, the military school centre, the logistics bases, our protection regiment; and the IKM of the Main Staff is also informed, that is, the IKMs that had been established.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show you Exhibit 5D1325.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: General, as you can see, this is an order from a document of the Eastern Bosnia Corps. Could you tell us how it happened, how this order was generated?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order from my command directed to the Posavina tactical group; and, in the preamble you can see that we are informing them of the reception of a telegram of the following content, and it is then quoted there in its entirety. So it's the entire text of the order of the Main Staff, and we also added our own measures to make this order even more serious. In the central part, you can see that it says up there "trajno", "permanently," and we excepted the cease-fire to turn into peace. So we anticipated that this document would be archived for a longer period of time rather than destroyed. Certain commissions were established at that period. The Main Staff established a commission in each corps, including mine, and I had to inform the subordinated units that they could come unexpectedly, suddenly, to check whether this order is be respected.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, if we can turn page 4 in the English and page 2 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We can see the name of Slavko Guzvic. Do you remember this officer?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is item 6 in the B/C/S version. It's the commission in my corps. There is the chairman, General Budimir Gavric; and the other members are Colonels Lukic and Guzvic, and Lieutenant-Colonel Milan Gavric and a representative of the civilian authorities as this was ordered from the zone. Guzvic was an officer in my corps at the Majevica brigade; and, later on, he was a liaison officer with UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would just like to Republic of Slovenia to page 1 of this document. We can see that this document was sent to TG Posavina. How is it that we do not see -- that we see on this document that it was only sent to TG Posavina?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a telegram. This is a document which is given to the hands of someone. In the integral document, it reads: "Delivered to the commands," and so-and-so. Here, it must be entered manually to which unit it was delivered, and each brigade or regiment or independent battalion which belongs to the East Bosnian Corps must receive one of these, a copy of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to remain a little longer on the issue of the agreement and show you a document that I believe you've never seen. It's the same cease-fire agreement which was sent by the Main Staff of the army of Bosnia Herzegovina to the corps of this army, 5D1352. What I am interested in this document is on page 2; page 2 in the English version, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: If you could read paragraph that begins with: [In English] "Predict points from which the Chetniks should withdraw."

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I read it out loud?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this confirms my previous statement. The army was Bosnia and Herzegovina did not have sincere intentions. They did not want the cease-fire to grow into peace. Here, they are trying to portray their defeat on Bjelasnica and Igman, and annul it by taking over some dominant positions from the army of Republika Srpska, who would give it over to UNPROFOR, and then they would take it over from them. This actually came through, and this proves that they wanted to go on waging this war for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In this order, we see the term "Chetnik" several times. Does this also surprise you?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an official document. I am really surprised to see this term which you may be used in propaganda documents. But in an official document, we would always refer to them as the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and we would also mention the number of unit, or, sometimes, we would refer to them as Muslims. I would never refer to them as Balije or Ustasha. This is part of the jargon. Obviously, this is down to the practices or culture of the operative organ or somebody in the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina who drafted this.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Earlier, we mentioned Colonel Slavko Guzvic, and you said that he was appointed as the liaison officer with international organisations such as UNPROFOR. Was this colonel in your corps throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe that in 1995 or towards the end of 1994, he received an order of the commander of the Main Staff, and he left the corps and was appointed as the liaison officer with UNPROFOR, and he was affiliated with the UNPROFOR staff in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So was he at Gornji Vakuf the whole time or another location too?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was there until the moment he was expelled.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show you Exhibit 5D760.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This is the order from the Main Staff through which Colonel Guzvic is appointed liaison officer of the Republika Srpska army, but here the Dubrave airfield mentioned. Does this mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were some talks about him going there, but I don't remember him going, actually. The time plays a role here, Your Honours. He left my unit, so I really can't remembered whether he was, indeed, deployed to the Dubrave airfield where he was supposed to control the aircraft that landed there and was misused for the armament of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you said that he was expelled from the place where he was based as a liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to show you 5D761.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the previous document, the army -- of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina that I saw for the first time, at one point they say, "We will not allow for the representatives of Chetniks to be deployed in the UNPROFOR bases in our territory, and this is something that the UNPROFOR should be aware of." Obviously, this is the implementation without the consent of the Main Staff for any previous agreements. They had agreed our mission consisting of liaison officers to leave Gornji Vakuf, and they did it without the previous consent of the Main Staff. Then the Main Staff ordered for them to be handcuffed, put on a helicopter, and transported over to our side. That was a forcible deportation of a mission which is on -- which is unprecedented under any normal circumstances, because, as a matter of fact, they were there as a military attache, and they should have enjoyed a diplomatic status as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you have personal knowledge of what you're saying, or does your information come from this document, or do you have another source of information?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My officer returned to the corps command after having been expelled from that mission, and he told us that he felt humiliated and he put us in the picture. He told us what had happened. Obviously, the UNPROFOR command thought, so every BiH army which [as interpreted] is their command -- and all that time they were ignoring any other civilized norms, because they had originally requested for that mission to be present at their staff in Gornji Vakuf. That mission was established at their request in order to coordinate certain problems in order to deal with any problems that might arise between the UNPROFOR and the army of Republika Srpska, or any problems that might arise during the implementation of the cease-fires.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. If I could draw your attention to lines 18, particularly lines 19 and to the next two lines, anyway. The witness -- I am not understanding what we have in the transcript, basically. He told us he is referring to his officer, okay, who felt humiliated et cetera. "He told us what had happened. Obviously, the UNPROFOR command thought, so every BiH army which is their command --" and there is something missing. "And all that time they were ignoring any civilized norms, because they had originally requested for that mission to be present at their staff in Gornji Vakuf." What I don't understand is the part saying, "Obviously, the UNPROFOR command thought, so every BiH army which is their command -- " I don't understand it, if you could assist. It's probably a question of the witness going too fast and the interpreters not be becoming all to cope, but if you could deal with it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the UNPROFOR command requests from the Main Staff to send a group of officers that would have been present all the time at the command post of UNPROFOR in Gornji Vakuf, in order to coordinate their mutual activities and faster resolution of possible misunderstandings. All of a sudden and unilaterally, the UNPROFOR command, without any previous agreements or negotiations with the Main Staff, expelled that mission of ours under the pretext that their safety was at threat. In the UNPROFOR base, with over 1.000 soldiers, how could anybody's safety and security come under threat? In the previous document that I was shown, drafted by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in one of the passages, it says, "Ask from UNPROFOR to make Chetnik officers leave the UNPROFOR bases on our territory." Gornji Vakuf was on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is clear that the UNPROFOR command gave in to the pressures and unilaterally expelled our mission, they terminated their stay. I hope that I have been able to clarify. If you wish me to provide you with anymore details, I am at your disposal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think I can agree with my learned colleague that what we had in, Mr. President, in your line citation was a simple mishearing. What I heard was "...every BiH army wish is their command..." I think that's what the General said and what was mistranscribed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter confirms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You've already mentioned the problems that you encountered in Majevica in the spring of 1995. Do you have any information about problems of cease-fire violation -- violation of cease-fire agreements on other fronts?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, there was an offensive on Mount Vlasic that was launched by the BiH army against the units of the 1st Krajina Corps during the cease-fire. There were a series of other individual violations of cease-fire attempts to correct certain defence lines and certain positions. The army of Republika Srpska was standing completely still at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you recall when this cease-fire violation occurred in Vlasic more or less?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was either before the new year 1995 or the beginning of 1995. It was in the area of responsibility of the 1st Corps. I can't tell you exactly. I had my own zone of responsibility. I was elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show witness Exhibit 5D1212. This is the information regarding the enemy offensive at Vlasic, and it's not very clear in the title of the document, but then we can see 24, 25, 295.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could this document describe the offensive at Vlasic that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And in the upper part where you had the date, you can see that it was drafted in March, and it speaks of the offensive that had taken place the month before. This information was drafted on the 7th of March and reports on what had happened on Mount Vlasic the month before.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would now like to return to your area in Majevica. The cease-fire violations in Majevica, were they reported in your combat reports?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to show the witness Exhibit 5D1140. This is the daily report of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska. If we could go to page 2 both in the B/C/S and English versions, what I'm interested in is paragraph 4, zone of responsibility of the Eastern Bosnia Corps. Indeed, we see that this report refers to an attack on the Majevica section of the front.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I don't expect you to recall precisely what was indicated in your report, but could you tell us where the Main Staff derived the information that is in this report which is the report of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I have received a wrong interpretation or whether your interpretation was wrong. This is not a report to the Main Staff. This is the Main Staff reporting to the Supreme Command and describing the situation on the entire battlefield; and under number 4, you will see my signature. The situation was dramatic, and I remember it very well because I had to go there. I had to go into the field. This was not just a minor provocation. This was a well-conceived, well-prepared, well-organised attack by two brigades whose intention was to take the Majevica plateau and create conditions which towers around the -- above the whole area. They wanted to proceed towards Ugljevik, Lopare, and Semberija. That was their planned direction of attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a 20-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau. The next break will be at noon exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would now like to show the witness Exhibit 5D1141. This is another report from the Main Staff, dated the 22nd of March 1995. We would need to refer to page 2. We are still on the attacks by the Bosnia and Herzegovina army at Majevica. We see that the relay at Stolice is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you tell us what type of relay this is. What is this about?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, on the top of Mount Majevica -- and the peek is called Stolice. At the top of that mountain, there was a radio and television relay station. It was not a military facility, but that facility made possible the transmission of images from the central television at Pale to the territory of the entire Republika Srpska. It is also a hub of civilian communications.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So, in these series of reports, I would like to show you 5D1142. And before this report arrives, I would like to know whether a unit not belonging to your corps was, for some reason, to be found in the area of your corps? Did you refer to that in the reports that you sent to the staff -- in the reports that you sent to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned everything that went on in the zone of the corps to my -- in my reports to the Main Staff; and if there is a unit belonging to another command, I mention it. Some units could transit through my zone, then I make mention of that, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So this is the report dated 23rd of March, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if we could see page 2, at the very bottom of the page in B/C/S, we refer to a unit of the Drina Corps, the 10th Sabotage Detachment and police units.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it possible for the 2nd [as interpreted] Sabotage Unit to operate in your zone without you mentioning it in the reports sent to the Main Staff? Would it be --

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are speaking about the 10th Sabotage Unit, and that's the unit of the Main Staff. That unit was sent -- was deployed to my area to help me, because it was the critical at Majevica. And without that unit and without police units, it would have been difficult for us to retake that territory. And when they come to my zone, they are resubordinated to me; that is, my command, bearing in mind that the police have their own commander. But he coordinates his activities with me, and they are deployed as security forces for my logistics.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you specify the situation at the moment? Could you tell us what you said in your last sentence where you referred to the police?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said earlier, under the conditions when the state of war has not been declared, the Main Staff does not command police units; the Minister of the Interior does. This unit came under the approval of the Minister of the Interior to help my units at Majevica. They cooperate with us in the direction that I determine, but when they come and when they return, as well as their line of command, is not within my purview. It is up to me only to incorporate them into combat activities, and I -- it is up to me to supply them with food, ammunition, and band aid, et cetera. If the state of war had been declared, they would have become a part of the armed forces, and orders would be issued to them in the same way as to the military. In this way, they could have said after two days that they are leaving to carry out another task, and I wouldn't have been able to stop them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Let's get back to what I am interested in. More specifically, we can see that you drafted a report and that the units arrived. When, for instance, as far as the 10th Sabotage Detachment was concerned, when this detachment arrived in your area, could it happen that you did not inform the Main Staff about this?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only if they came in plain clothes, but that unit is a regular unit. Although they are a sabotage detachment, they had their specific tasks and duties and they should not arrive without my approval.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you have the duty to inform the Main Staff about their arrival?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, they were, indeed, sent to me by the Main Staff, and I said that they had been included in combat activities. That is a normal military sequence of activities. In this case, the Main Staff was in a critical condition which can be seen from the fact they deployed this unit which is not an offensive unit, but they had nothing else to send to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I am now talking about another topic. What was the relationship between the army of Republika Srpska and UNPROFOR at the beginning of the war in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The relations between UNPROFOR and the VRS varied depending on whether they were neutral or whether they were totally partial in favour of the army of BiH. Initially, they were neutral; but, later on, even the UNHCR engaged in some activities that are not appropriate for a humanitarian organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show you document 5D763. This is an order coming from the Main Staff of the army of the Republika Srpska relating to UNPROFOR, dated 23rd of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In paragraphs 2 and 3, we can see what the position of the army of the Republika Srpska was as contained in this order, and we can see in the last sentence of paragraph 3 that it says: "They have nothing against checks of every convoy or individual vehicle or the rooms and buildings they use." Do you know why such controls were made?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it on television; and, later on, it came from a report -- it came in a report from the Main Staff that ammunition was found in a convoy allegedly transporting humanitarian aid to Srebrenica and Sarajevo. Then the reputation of the UNPROFOR was damaged, not only in the eyes of the army but also in the people, so that even some women would three stones at their vehicles. Then a meeting was held with the UNPROFOR command, and they agreed that at certain checkpoints vehicles could be checked in order to eliminate any suspicion that they are transporting things they shouldn't be transporting.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You did talk about the reputation of this organisation that had been damaged in the eyes of the people.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we turn to page 2 of this document, please. If we look at item 5, we can see that this order mentions what the people have been doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did the military authorities have the authority to prevent such acts from occurring? I am talking about the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this says clearly: "Through the organs of authority and the SUP and the zone of responsibility of the corps, make sure that the population does not take adverse acts toward the representatives of international institutions." Here, probably the MUP was assigned some tasks too, and the civilian authorities sent out a warning through the local authorities; and the commander here obliges us to contact the MUP and the civilian authorities to prevent adverse acts on the parts of some civilians which could prevent convoys from passing, because the people were embittered.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show you document 5D764. This is a document stemming from the Main Staff of the army of the Republika Srpska, sent out to all the corps. What I am interested in is the penultimate paragraph on the first page in English. This has to do with -- well, this is the third line, the first paragraph on page 3 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: According to this paragraph, "The corps commands shall undertake measures to explain properly to our army members, citizens, why we allow humanitarian aid convoys organised by UNPROFOR to pass." This document was sent to your corps also. Did you have to deal with this kind of matter?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was fortunate enough to have very few convoys passing through my territory; and, here, I was informed as a neighbour of the Drina Corps, I suppose. They just wanted to inform me about the problems that they had encountered in their work.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to move to 1995 and show you another order stem from the Main Staff dated the 12th of March 1995 which was also sent out to all the corps. This is document 5D852. I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you look at paragraph 1 of this document, please. You have already said that the relationship with UNPROFOR changed and varied. As far as you were concerned, was this a general belief in 1995 as regards UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, this relationship was at a very low level in 1995 due to various abuses and unequal treatment accorded to the BiH army, on the one hand, and the VRS on the other -- or, rather, the civilian population. It happened that they did send humanitarian aid to the territory of Republika Srpska, but there are also cases that the civilian population refused to take the aid. They were disappointed because that aid was not even 10 per cent of the aid that was given to the population in the territory under the control of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, if you look at paragraph 2, this has to do with criminal acts which had been comitted against UNPROFOR members.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could now move to page 2 in English, and if we can show the witness the bottom of this first page and then page 2. We can see that an investigation and prosecution was underway against these criminals.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: According to you, was this the only order of this kind that you ever received during the war, or were there others as well?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a drastic warning, but there were others on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said that the convoys did not go through our territory. Nonetheless, did you have any contacts with humanitarian aid organisations?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were very few such passages, but I had other humanitarian organisations. I had a commiserate for refugees on my territory. I had the ICRC which performed its duties honourably, there were Medecins Sans Frontieres, and so on and so forth. There were some attempts -- well, you know, let me put it this way: There are criminals who may be under the impression that a free for all license was given to them when they such treatments were accorded to other institutions. For example, on my territory, they seized a four drive wheel vehicle from the ICRC, and we located it only two days later. It had already been painted in different colours, and we returned it to the ICRC. I believe that this was a case of abuse that resulted from their anger towards the ICRC, but there was no reason to be angry with the ICRC because they were really an honourable organisation and true do-gooders.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You mentioned these vehicles that had been stolen, ICRC vehicles, and the attitude you had vis-a-vis this act. Was this attitude the same amongst other members of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, that was the case. There were individuals who stood out from the rest, but those were criminals who were engaged in criminal activities, and they were prosecuted in accordance with the law. If you are referring to the enemy side, the army of BiH, I personally was not convinced that they abided by all the rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You mentioned those vehicles that had been stolen from the ICRC and painted over in another colour. Did the reverse happen also; in other words, when standard vehicles had been painted white to demonstrate that this was an aid organisation when, in fact, these were military vehicles?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would be something that is prescribed by the Geneva Conventions and rules of war, and it has to be punished. It has to be militarily punished.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show you Exhibit number 5D1002. This is an order dated the 5th of November 1992 which mentions this situation precisely where UN vehicles had been used for other things.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you remember whether this order was in effect in 1995?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in effect, this law on the ban to paint vehicles in different colours. That was in effect, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show you a document from the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, 5D1358.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Please take the time you need to read this. Did you have occasion to observe such events among the ranks of the army of Bosnia Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never seen this document before; but, interestingly enough, it does not forbid people from painting in different colours, or over-painting, but from publically showing them. The BiH army used this type of masking on a large scale because nobody opened fire on such aircraft. It says here that it should not be publically shown because it is detrimental, but it doesn't say that over-painting such vehicles or aircraft is forbidden, or that it shouldn't be done.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You have already mentioned the ICRC and your contacts with the ICRC in the army of the Republika Srpska. The subordinate units that were subordinated to the Main Staff of the army of the Republika Srpska, well, the contacts or relationship with ICRC, was this regulated by anything, by an order?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very beginning of the war, an order came with this regard. We had to study this order, and we had to study the Geneva Conventions together with all the foot soldiers and officers. As far as my corps is concerned, in the place where the corps command was, there was their regional office, an office of the ICRC; and in all the other places, they had their branch offices. We had regular contacts with them. I had a liaison officer, Lieutenant-Colonel Demirovic, who also held a Ph.D. in sociology. He was in constant contact with the ICRC, and, once a month, they would come and meet me personally. They called this occasion a "Tea with the General." Then we would discuss any issues, any problems that they encountered in their work. I am, indeed, grateful for all their effort and all the assistance they extended to us during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You mentioned an order which was issued at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to show you 5D1001. This is an order stemming from the Main Staff dated the 30th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you recognise this order?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise this document. This is the order that I've just referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did this order remain in effect through the entire period of the war?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You mentioned the arms and munitions that were transported in the convoys. I would like to show you a short excerpt of a video that was shot by the BBC.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is 5D1391. Can we show this video, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: "Journalist: The UN aid convoy had been stopped at a checkpoint in the Bosnia Serb held suburb of Ilija. It was carrying flour loaded at the airport nearby to the Muslim held village of Butmir. The undeclared ammunition was discovered wedged between the pallets of food aid and the truck bed. Serbian soldiers found more than 5.000 rounds of ammunition for rifles and for heavy machine guns. "The Serbs have said to have reacted to the arms find with fury. The French officer commanding the escort remained with the Serbs in Ilija for several hours afterwards, while UN officials searched the airport. In an aid depot, they found more rifle and machine-gun ammunition and a quantity of explosives. "Male: I find it deplorable and, indeed, very sad as well that anybody should attempt to use in United Nations humanitarian aid mission in an attempt to smuggle munitions. "Journalist: The UNHCR said it regrets the incident, but in a war situation, such things are bound to happen from time to time, and all sides have a vested interest in trying to get things transported in any way possible. "Male: What is possible? "Female: I think everything is possible. This is -- "Male: In terms of getting weapons onto one of your lorries, what will be possible? "Female: Well, it's pretty difficult because we have pretty rigorous checking exercises, but, clearly, what this shows, I think, is that we can't leave these trucks for five minutes. "Journalist: This arms find, while genuinely regulated by the UNHCR, could do untold damage towards relief operations, many of which rely on the goodwill and cooperation of the Bosnian Serbs. Their leaders have on several occasions accused the UN of supplying the Muslims with weapons "Dozens of aid convoys cross Serbian lines in Bosnia every day. Now Bosnian Serb politicians say, regretfully, they will have to make checkpoint controls and searches must stricter than they wanted to "Male: That's too bad, because that makes convoy -- that makes them keep longer at our checkpoints. For the time being, we wouldn't like to do anything else because we think now the humanitarian side at this moment has to be strictly divided from the political side. "Journalist: As they await the outcome of their investigations into the arms find, UN aid officials say they will increase their own security measures to try and ensure this incident is never repeated. "George Eaton, BBC News, Belgrade."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I am waiting for translation of the transcript of the video to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... it has to stop there. Sorry for the interpreters, I had my microphone off. My apologies. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you. We'll stipulate that the date of the video is 8 April 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Incidentally, while we are at it, in the course of Madam Fauveau's examination-in-chief, my feeling is that she asked a lot of questions on issues which I, personally, don't believe are contested by the Prosecution. As we go along - and this applies not only to her but with this witness but also to other witnesses - if there are areas where you are in a position to stipulate, it will be extremely helpful, it will cut down on the time, and it will avoid you having to ask questions because an issue as been raised. So it's an invitation which I am making to you, take it or leave it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we get back to 25.55 on this video.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: "Journalist: Bosnian Serb politicians say, regretfully, they will have to make checkpoint controls and searches much stricter than they wanted to. "Male: It's too bad because that makes convoy -- that makes them keep longer at our checkpoints. For the time being ..." "Journalist: "... cross Serbian lines in Bosnia ..." -- "Male: "... convoy -- that he makes them" --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: General, do you recognise this man?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is Dr. Koljevic, a presidency member.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you tell us what he was a president of?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a member of the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he was also a member of the presidency of Republika Srpska later on. We were informed that he was in charge of international and humanitarian organisations in the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would now like to discuss with you the situation with UNPROFOR end of May 1995. Do you remember an incident in particular which occurred with UNPROFOR at the end of May 1995?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You'll have to help me and pinpoint the exact incident. There were several.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show you document P2669A. Can we show the witness paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We are discussing a member of the UNPROFOR that was taken prisoner. Does this remind you anything?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a bad decision. It was caused by the bombardment of our positions; and, here, the command of the Main Staff ordered us to take over some of the prisoners and to deploy them in our sector -- or, rather, to accommodate them in our sector and guarantee them safety. We received 27 members, my commander did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know where these UNPROFOR members were captured?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not taken in my territory. They came from the territory of the Romanija Sarajevo Corps, and I didn't want to take them to the prisoner of war camps, so I deployed them in my artillery unit to be there together with my soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: How long did these UNPROFOR members stay in the area of your corps?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Short -- they stayed a short time, only five to seven days.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show the witness 5D1335. This is an order coming from President Karadzic which has to do with the liberation of 120 people, 120 members of UNPROFOR that had been captured. The date is that of the 2nd of June 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What I am interested in is this: You see this comment made and it is handwritten - unfortunately, it has not been translated into English - where it says --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the document in B/C/S so that we can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What I am surprised by is why does this say that this is strictly personal and why is it only sent to General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am surprised, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show you document 5D1337.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This is an order which was addressed to you and all the corps and your corps also.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see here that it isn't only to the attention of General Tolimir. The commander is also issuing an order, so he is familiar with it. This says that I should handover 26 prisoners, and I had received had 27. One was ill and was put up in hospital. He had left earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Well, this person who was sent to hospital, which hospital are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That member was first examined by the military doctor, and then he was transferred to the civilian hospital in Bijeljina, from where he was sent to the UNPROFOR hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you look at paragraph 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English, this is on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We are here talking about the prisoners that were in the area of the Drina Corps. There were six of them in the hospital of the Main Staff and five which were in the Vlasenica barracks.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to these people? Do you know anything about it at all?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were handed over, all of them. They were all handed over on that same occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show you 5D1338.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a handwritten record stating that my officer handed over UNPROFOR members, because I said to him not to return without a written document. There were no conditions to typewrite it as this was at a border crossing, so he wrote it by hand because he couldn't return to me without a receipt, a document, stating that he had handed over the members. You can see here that their equipment is listed and their armaments.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said that it was on the frontier crossing, but if you look at all the names, we can see that it's the Karakaj-Zvornik barracks, and I think the word "Zvornik" is omitted in the English version. Do you have any recollection that the officers of your zone were taken to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had left in the direction of Zvornik, but I understood that they were handed over at the border crossing. I might be wrong, but I don't think it changes anything in the essence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the witness page 2 of this document; page 2 in the English version, too. We see several names at the foot of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Amongst these names, do you recognise anyone?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one who handed them over is my officer from my security organ, it's Lieutenant Cvijan Kurtuma, and I don't know the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you recall what the situation was on the Sarajevo front in June 1995?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that a large scale offensive was in progress from the direction of Sarajevo toward our forces of the Romanija Corps, probably to meet with the forces from the direction of Srebrenica and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did your corps have certain obligations that were imposed on it in respect of this situation in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you have seen, I received help for Majevica. Under the same way, I first deployed a light brigade and then another battalion to help out because the situation was critical. It's normal in the military to regroup and to send help to the most threatened spots.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I'd like to show you 5D1155. It's an order of the 15th of June, 1995. 1155. [In English] 5D1165. [Interpretation] 5D1165.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the order for me to send a unit to the area of Butile.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In item 2, we also see that the Drina Corps also sent a unit at that time. Was this unit from your corps the only one to be sent to the zone of the Sarajevo Corps at that time?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order pertains only to the Bijeljina Light Infantry Brigade, but the situation became even more complex later, and I had to send an additional battalion and I had to obey. The situation was not great with me either, but there, at the Romanija plateau, it was even worse.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see Exhibit 5D1217.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: At item 1, we see the command of the 1st Krajina Corps. If we could move to page 2 in English. At the foot of the page 1 in B/C/S, 1st Krajina Corps and Drina Corps to send a unit. And on page 2 in B/C/S, page 3 in the English version, item 3, it's the other unit that you've just referred to.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The situation was critical and the unit had to leave as soon as possible because there were heavy losses that the -- that the units of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps were suffering.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know where General Milovanovic was in July, August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, from the strategic point of view, it is obvious that the army of BiH was trying to improve its positions by using all of the forces available before the beginning of the peace negotiations and to reduce the percentage of the territory under the control of the VRS, so that they had launched offensive activities in the Herzegovina; around Sarajevo; at Majevica, they had started earlier; at Vlasic. The Bihac Corps had also received a signal to start combat activities, and then General Milovanovic had to go personally to the Krajina and establish an IKM. I sent a battalion there, too, to help them, because the offensive had to be stopped, because the territory of Bosnia Krajina was on the brink of being severed into two parts. So the situation was critical everywhere, and we expected peace. It was a great surprise to us. It seems that we had trusted them too much. They had put a signature on a document stating their intentions, but probably they were not sincere.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: General Milovanovic was in Krajina on the western front of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Who was the head of the army staff of the Republika Srpska? Who was the head of the Main Staff Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head -- sorry. The Chief of Staff? The Chief of Staff was General Milovanovic. He was in the territory of Republika Srpska. In the zone of any combat activity, he was always chief. He was not incapable of working. So wherever he was, he was always Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know where during that period in August 1995 where General Mladic was?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know precisely. I believe that for a while he took part in some negotiations; but, basically, he was also in the zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you say "he was in the zone," is there a specific zone that you are thinking of?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, every command has its zone of responsibility. The entire Republika Srpska is the zone of responsibility of the Main Staff. I have an area for my corps. If I leave it, I am no longer in my area or zone; but the commander or Chief of Staff, they are always in their territory, in their zone, if they are in the Republika Srpska, because their zone of responsibility encompasses the entire Republika Srpska. That's the zone that I meant. I hope that you understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know if General Mladic at one point in August 1995 was in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember; he may have been.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Only answer this question, if you can: If General Mladic and General Milovanovic were together in Krajina, or the army of Republika Srpska was taking important decisions -- where the army of Republika Srpska was taking important decisions?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When things were getting complicated in the Krajina, it wasn't only Milovanovic who went there. All the assistants of General Mladic went there, and even he personally to help at the site because the situation was disastrous. The Republika of Krajina, the joint forces, the combined forces, the regular forces of the Republic of Croatia, and the army of B&H, together with HVO forces, had launched a general offensive against the Krajina municipalities. There, the decisive battle for Republika Srpska's very existence was being waged. They may not have been there all the time, but probably they met occasionally. I know that General Milovanovic didn't have a sufficient number of officers. I sent my assistant for morale, Colonel Jelacic, to see my unit which had been deployed there, to see if everything was all right. I sent them some ammunition and food and also some personnel. But when they arrived there, I got a telegram: "This is just the man I need, I'll keep him here. And from now on, he is considered to be a member of the IKM of the Main Staff." They practically captured my assistant. Later on, Colonel Beronja went there and he was also kept there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: During this period, when most of the officers of the Main Staff in Krajina, were important decisions taken in Krajina or Crna Rijeka? I would -- answer this question only if you know the answer.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if the commander with most of his most senior assistants is at a certain place, who can take important decisions at the place where the staff was normally? There was no one left to do that. Wherever the commander establishes his command, that is the main command post, and the site at Crna Rijeka became a reserve post. The command is always at the place where the commander is.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I have just a few more questions for you. Did you know that the combat had been conducted around Srebrenica? When did you have knowledge of the fighting around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I must say with regret that I didn't know that this operation was being planned at all. Although it was in my vicinity, I was surprised and, in a way, I was hurt. When combat activities started and we could hear intensive artillery fire, I ordered one of my officer to inquire with the Drina Corps what this was about, and we received a reply that those were regular activities. Then after that, for some three days, it was quite, only to start again with even more intensity. And from television, we learned that the operation around Srebrenica had started, and General Milovanovic [as interpreted] could be seen, et cetera. We were not informed of those activities at all, which is not in line with the military rules and rules of information.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: During this period, July 1995, did you have any contact with General Miletic? And just before you answer, on page 43, line 24, the witness says "General Mladic." Did you have contacts with General Miletic during this period of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday, in a jocular fashion, that the occasions were rare when General Miletic left the Main Staff, because all the information went to him and he drafted reports. So everybody else could go places, and he was always on duty. So when no one else was there, he could always be found there. You saw in one of those reports that one of my units was taken prisoner in the Lisaca region, and I had to organise an exchange with the 2nd Corps from Tuzla. We always exchanged prisoners on a basis of all for all; and, throughout the war, we had a very good cooperation although we were enemies. But then a young commander had come in. Before him, there was a General Hasim Sabic, who secretly held meetings with me at the demarcation line, and he was later replaced by a -- by one Sead Delic. When he heard that I was no longer in possession of Batkovici because I had handed over all prisoners, and he had refused to exchange --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: If you could speak a little more slowly, it is not properly recorded in the transcript. You had Petkovic, and I think you said something else.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Batkovici, Batkovici. Your Honours, I get carried away. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I don't think that the witness said "I was no longer in possession of Batkovici." He said something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then ask him straight away, please, madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can reply, Your Honours. There is no need for Ms. Fauveau to ask me. Batkovici was in my territory, but three times I completely emptied it and shut it down. I didn't have enough prisoners to handover 90 prisoners for 90 of my people. That's why I called up the Main Staff, and General Miletic answered the phone. I asked him to give me 90 people for -- to exchange them. I asked him about the combat activities, and he said to me bitterly that he doesn't pass on information to anyone, because he's constantly being called up from the Supreme Command about what had been achieved, and he didn't know what to say to them. Then I asked him to put me through to General Mladic, which he did. Unfortunately, General Mladic said that they didn't have any prisoners of war, and he had no time to continue talking to me and he hung up.
